_meta.title: BGP route visibility and path analysis runbook - Topolograph
_meta.description: Load the Topolograph BGP demo, inspect BMP sessions and routes, understand RIB visibility, and verify BGP best-path decisions and next-hop resolution.
_meta.meta_keywords: BGP visualization, BMP RFC 7854, BMP RFC 8671, BMP RFC 9069, BGP best path, BGP route reflector
_meta.og_title: BGP route visibility and path analysis runbook
_meta.og_description: A practical Topolograph runbook for BGP sessions, RIB visibility, best-path decisions, and BGP next-hop resolution over OSPF.

page_title: BGP route visibility and path analysis
page_intro: Use the built-in demo to inspect the route view Topolograph can prove, verify a best-path decision, compare route state over time, and follow a BGP next hop through OSPF.
demo_intro: The generated BGP demo loads automatically. It contains 13 routers, 22 BGP sessions, and two route reflectors with deliberately different BMP capabilities.
demo_steps: Confirm that the generated demo topology is present; no upload or manual demo load is required.
Open General View and confirm that the BGP overlay is visible. The overlay is enabled by default; the control can hide and restore it.
Find RR1 (7854) and RR2 (7854+9069+8671). Their labels identify the BMP information each reflector exports.
demo_result: The IGP topology remains the base graph. The BGP overlay adds sessions without replacing OSPF connectivity.
sessions_intro: Use both representations: the table is precise for filtering, while the overlay confirms where the selected session sits in the topology.
sessions_steps: Open BGP Sessions and filter by peer 123.123.31.31.
Confirm that the PE has one session, to RR1, and no session to RR2.
Return to General View and locate the same PE-to-RR1 adjacency in the BGP overlay.
sessions_visual: The filtered BGP Sessions table below makes the RFC 7854 limitation case concrete: PE31 has one observed session, to RR1.
sessions_alt: BGP Sessions table filtered for PE31, showing its only session to RR1
sessions_result: This single-homed PE is the deliberate RFC 7854 limitation case used later in the runbook.
visibility_title: 3. Know which RIB view you are using
visibility_intro: A BMP session with a route reflector does not automatically expose every peer's installed table. Topolograph records the strongest view supported by the available feed and states any inference needed to calculate a path.

selective_export_note: RR2 exports post-policy Adj-RIB-Out only for selected peers. This is valid: BMP Adj-RIB-Out monitoring is configured per peer and address family, even though BGP itself maintains an Adj-RIB-Out for every established peer.
all_routes_intro: Start from the graph-wide BGP Routes table before narrowing to one router. This is the place to inspect and filter the route data collected for the whole demo.
all_routes_steps: Open Graph table and select BGP Routes. Leave the table in Live mode.
Confirm that no node scope is shown. This is the graph-wide route collection, not a router card's resolved view.
Use the prefix, BMP source, RIB, peer, or path-attribute columns to find the route set you want to investigate.
all_routes_visual: The full-screen Live table below is the graph-wide BGP Routes view. It is the starting point before a node card or a route filter narrows the scope.
all_routes_alt: Full-screen graph-wide BGP Routes table in Live mode
all_routes_result: Pass: BGP Routes opens as the graph-wide entry point. The following sections deliberately narrow that view to a router only when the question requires it.
node_card_title: 5. Read the route view on a node card
node_card_intro: The route count on a node now follows the resolved RIB view for that router. It no longer adds together every stored BMP row that happens to name the router.
node_card_steps: Click PE14 (123.14.14.14) on the graph and find the BGP section of its node card.
Confirm Routes is 4 and read the explanation: the routes were advertised by RR2 (123.123.101.101) to this router through RFC 8671.
Read the RIB breakdown. Adj-RIB-Out (post) describes RR2's exported RIB; from PE14's perspective these four advertisements are its inferred Adj-RIB-In.
Do not add the separate advertised count to Routes. Advertised means what the selected router sent to peers, not what its own resolved route view contains.
node_card_alt: PE14 node card showing four routes advertised by RR2 and an Adj-RIB-Out post-policy breakdown
node_card_visual: This card is PE14's resolved view: four routes inferred from RR2's post-policy Adj-RIB-Out export.
node_card_result: Pass: PE14 shows four routes, one directional RIB breakdown, and an explicit observation source. The count does not include PE14 advertisements received by the route reflectors or unrelated reflector Loc-RIB rows.
routes_title: 6. Filter, sort, and page through one node's routes
routes_intro: Open the route drawer from the node card so the table starts with the same resolved RIB scope rather than an unrelated graph-wide collection.
routes_steps: Click Routes 4 on PE14. Confirm the drawer contains exactly 100.30.0.0/24, 10.100.31.0/24, 2001:db8:123:123:30:30::/96, and 2001:db8:100:31::/64.
Filter prefix by 100.30.0.0/24. Matching rows and the table counter must both fall from 4 to 1.
Clear filters and confirm all four PE14 routes return. Clearing a table filter must not remove the node scope that the card established.
Click a sortable heading such as prefix, next hop, Local Preference, or MED. Repeated clicks cycle ascending, descending, and unsorted; address columns use address order, not text order.
Use Rows per page for large route tables. The demo has only one page in this node-scoped example, so the previous and next controls correctly remain disabled.
routes_alt: PE14 route table filtered from four routes to the prefix 100.30.0.0/24
routes_visual: The table below retains the PE14 scope and adds the prefix filter, leaving one matching route.
routes_result: Pass: the filtered row names RR2 as the BMP source and Adj-RIB-Out (post) as the observed direction. Filters are server-side, so Matching rows describes the whole scoped result, not only the current page.
best_path_intro: The demo isolates one decision step per prefix. Start with AS_PATH: inspect the competing attributes, then build the route from RR2 to prove which egress the path engine selects.
as_path_steps: Compare the two candidates: both have Local Preference 100, IGP origin, and MED 10. PE30 advertises AS_PATH 65010 65011 65012; PE14 advertises AS_PATH 65010.
Switch to BGP / VPN path mode. Set Router to RR2 (123.123.101.101), VPN or global table to global, and To to 198.18.2.0/24; then select Build a path.
In Route resolution, confirm the first row is BGP on RR2 with next hop PE14 (123.14.14.14). The remaining rows resolve that selected next hop through IGP.
as_path_candidates_alt: BGP route filters and the two AS_PATH candidates for 198.18.2.0/24
as_path_candidates_visual: The filtered BGP Routes table below shows the two candidates before route construction.
as_path_builder_alt: BGP VPN path builder set to RR2, the global table, and 198.18.2.0/24
as_path_builder_visual: Next, set the BGP / VPN path builder to RR2, the global table, and this prefix.
as_path_result_alt: Route resolution showing RR2's BGP decision with PE14 as the selected next hop
as_path_resolution_visual: The resulting Route resolution table starts with RR2's BGP selection of PE14; later rows are only the IGP underlay walk.
as_path_result: Pass: the post-policy candidates differ in AS_PATH length while Local Preference, Origin, and MED tie. Building the route from RR2 selects PE14 (123.14.14.14) as the BGP next hop; the following IGP rows only resolve reachability to that egress.
decision_rows: Lower MED from the same neighboring AS
Different neighboring AS values make MED ineligible
Lower originator ID after earlier ties
advanced_text: The demo deliberately proves six early decision steps. Later tie-breakers such as eBGP over iBGP, IGP cost to next hop, route age, cluster-list length, and peer address remain reference cases rather than claims demonstrated by this snapshot.
compare_title: 8. Compare route state between two instants
compare_intro: Live shows the current route table. Compare reconstructs the table at T0 and T1 and reports only the net difference between those two instants.
compare_steps: Open the graph-wide BGP Routes table and switch from Live to Compare.
Keep the default one-hour T0 to T1 window created when the demo loads, then press Run.
Confirm one added route: 100.14.210.0/24. The changed-at value identifies the event that last touched the route.
Read added, withdrawn, and changed as endpoint outcomes. Intermediate churn that returns to the same state is not a net difference.
Switch back to Live to restore the server-paged current table.
compare_alt: BGP route Compare mode showing 100.14.210.0/24 as added in the default one-hour window
compare_visual: The comparison below is the endpoint difference for the default demo window, not a chronological event log.
compare_result: Pass: the default demo window is never empty and reports 100.14.210.0/24 as added, with MED 80 in the T1 state. Compare does not replace Live; it is a temporary unpaged result.
events_intro: Events uses the same BGP Routes drawer and time range, but preserves every route and peer observation instead of reducing them to a T0-to-T1 difference.
events_steps: Switch from Compare to Events and keep a time window that covers the demo change burst.
Press Run and verify one route add, one peer down event, and one route change for 100.14.210.0/24.
Use the event, kind, prefix, peer, and timestamp columns to distinguish route churn from session state.
events_visual: The Events view below lists the observations chronologically: the added route, the peer-down event, then the changed route with MED 80.
events_alt: BGP Routes Events mode showing a route add, a peer down event, and a route change
events_result: Pass: Events shows all three observations in order. Unlike Compare, it keeps intermediate events even when the final route state is unchanged.
resolution_title: 9. Follow BGP next-hop resolution through OSPF
resolution_intro: BGP chooses the route; OSPF supplies reachability to the selected BGP next hop. The path view shows that handoff explicitly.
resolution_steps: In Standard / IGP path mode, use PE30 (123.123.30.30) as the source and 100.14.0.0/24 as the destination.
Inspect the selected BGP row and identify PE14 (123.14.14.14) as the egress next hop.
Open Route resolution and read the result from left to right: the first row is BGP with administrative distance 200 and next hop PE14.
Continue through the five IGP rows with administrative distance 110 that physically resolve reachability from PE30 to PE14.
resolution_alt: Route resolution table with one BGP decision followed by five IGP next-hop-resolution rows
resolution_visual: The table below separates the single BGP route choice from the IGP hops that make its next hop reachable.
resolution_result: Pass: BGP chooses PE14 as the egress once; OSPF then supplies the physical underlay walk. The table must not collapse that underlay into one summary row.
limits_intro: Filter for PE31 (123.123.31.31). Topolograph can show the routes that RR1 received from this PE, but RFC 7854 alone does not reveal which route PE31 installed or what RR1 advertised back to it.
limits_steps: Open the router's RIB summary and confirm view adj_rib_out with path calculation unavailable.
Try the same destination used in a buildable case and verify that no route is offered for path construction.
Compare PE31 with PE15: PE15 is also missing per-peer Adj-RIB-Out, but RR2 Loc-RIB permits a reflected view with explicit assumptions.
limits_result: No path is better than a path built from the wrong RIB. To remove this limit, provide the subject's Loc-RIB through RFC 9069 or its per-peer post-policy Adj-RIB-Out through RFC 8671.
